locator.quote: A classical algorithm cannot locate the winning column's certificate

feedback.feedback: The next clause says that an algorithm must spend the address cost in each of a constant fraction of the columns. Taken literally, this sounds like a necessary property of every successful execution. The proof establishes a distributional obstruction to bounded-error algorithms: a particular run can guess the correct cell cheaply.
feedback.why_it_matters: The abstract is often the only version of the classical mechanism a reader retains; it should not turn a probability estimate into a pathwise impossibility.
feedback.advice: Qualify the claim by bounded-error success on the planted experiment, or describe low-budget discovery as unlikely. Keep the per-column cost intuition.
feedback.prior_round_status: The body fixed the old CX010 overstatement by explaining prediction from query position; this residual is in the abstract, not the corrected body.

locator.quote: Together these give $R\approx Q^{4-2/k}$.

feedback.feedback: The approximation sign suggests a two-sided estimate for the complexities of the constructed function. What has actually been proved is a quantum upper bound and a randomized lower bound, enough to force a separation exponent. The same shorthand reappears in the overview displays.
feedback.why_it_matters: A separations specialist distinguishes a lower-bound witness from a tight characterization of that witness. The latter is stronger and is not needed here.
feedback.advice: Use one-sided separation language at the first occurrence and explicitly say that logarithms are suppressed in the overview.

locator.quote: reads its input one bit at a time

feedback.feedback: As a common opening for both models, this phrase gives a classical description immediately before introducing a quantum oracle that may query indices in superposition. The displayed oracle corrects the picture, but the opening sentence momentarily conflicts with it.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader entering from classical lower bounds should not have to mentally repair the first description of the comparison model.
feedback.advice: Describe the unit of cost as an oracle access to a bit-indexed input, then distinguish classical access and superposed quantum access without expanding the model discussion.

locator.quote: Taking $k=3$ in (2) gives exponent $10/3>3$

feedback.feedback: This is the right immediate consequence to give after the headline. It identifies an actual fixed parameter that beats the conjectured cube before moving to the limiting exponent.
feedback.why_it_matters: It prevents the reader from thinking that refuting the cubic conjecture already requires the technical growing-parameter remark.
feedback.advice: Keep this short calculation beside the conjecture and retain the later order of quantifiers.

locator.quote: This paper adds the following to the preprint.

feedback.feedback: The four-part contribution paragraph mixes the theorem, four exact constants, a proof-scope claim, two observations, the long record, and the formalisation. It reads like a project inventory just before the mathematical overview should establish momentum. The constants receive more opening space than their role warrants.
feedback.why_it_matters: The specialist needs to know which mechanism is new and which mathematical work this companion performs. Several competing selling points obscure that decision.
feedback.advice: Separate provenance and mathematical contribution from the quantitative-reference information. Keep the complete constant list at the theorem or in the sections where each constant is used.
feedback.prior_round_status: Round-six QX-017 asked for a shorter constants paragraph. The current detailed First/Second/Third/Fourth paragraph shows that the compression did not fully land.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm computes $g\circ h$ and Grover-checks a certificate

feedback.feedback: The certificate calculation appears abruptly. The important feature of AND–OR is that certifying all n inner outputs also certifies that the outer input lies in the domain of g. The supplied ABK intuition makes this domain-certification role explicit before performing the cost calculation.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without this connection, the paragraph looks like a fortuitous list of complexity measures rather than an explanation of why this particular inner function was chosen.
feedback.advice: Add the single causal link from n small certificates to certification of the outer promise. The resulting contrast with the present exact-circuit transcripts will then be immediate.

locator.quote: If $Q(g)$ is polylogarithmic

feedback.feedback: This assumption arrives after the displayed quantum bound that already uses it. For an arbitrary partial g, computing g composed with AND–OR contributes a factor Q(g) to the inner quantum cost; the preceding sentence initially introduces g without that restriction.
feedback.why_it_matters: The arithmetic is the explanation of why the earlier recipe reaches the cube. Its hypotheses should be attached before the formula is read, rather than supplied retroactively.
feedback.advice: State the polylogarithmic quantum-cost assumption when g is introduced, as ABK do by taking g to be Forrelation with Q(g)=1. This is a scope clarification, not a request for a new composition theorem.
feedback.prior_round_status: The round-six C05 conversion has been added. This concerns the placement of the new conversion's hypothesis, not its absence.

locator.quote: Exponent $a$ with $R=Q^{a}$ (total $f$)

feedback.feedback: The heading presents equality, but the entries record achieved separations up to logarithms and one universal upper bound. Those are different types of statement. The row labels partially repair this, but the heading is the part a reader is likely to quote.
feedback.why_it_matters: A compact history table should preserve the direction of each bound instead of relying on prose elsewhere to explain its shorthand.
feedback.advice: Name the first column as an achieved separation exponent and distinguish the universal upper-bound row visually or in a short note.

locator.quote: a separate cell $B_{i,s}$

feedback.feedback: The main construction figure draws one certificate array, that of the winner, while the lower bound depends on every column having a separate array. The text does say this, but the picture can still be remembered as one shared cheat sheet attached to the whole matrix.
feedback.why_it_matters: A shared array is precisely the mental model the new construction must displace; a misleading memory of the picture loses the source of the per-column charge.
feedback.advice: Add a compact indication that the omitted columns also carry their own A-blocks and cell arrays, or state this explicitly in the figure caption. Keep the winner's array enlarged.

locator.quote: Finding the erased zero means finding one marked zero

feedback.feedback: There are m easily encountered zeros in the dummy matrix, but only the zero in the independently chosen hidden column matters. Finding any zero costs about m queries; the m² scale comes from discovering enough distinct columns that the selected column is likely to be among them.
feedback.why_it_matters: The current sentence risks importing the wrong search problem at the very point where the extra factor m must become visible.
feedback.advice: Identify the marked zero as the zero in a hidden independently selected column, or use the discovery-count explanation from equation (11). Do not suggest that all zeros are interchangeable targets.

locator.quote: A query to $B_{i,s}$ reveals $s$ by its position

feedback.feedback: This now identifies the actual reduction. A simulator outputs the address named by a proposed query; it is not forced to read a certificate or decide whether it is valid. The sentence is substantially better than the informal assertion that a reader must first compute the address.
feedback.why_it_matters: The query-position observation is what turns a cell visit into an all-answers prediction event under a hard product law.
feedback.advice: Keep this sentence and its fuller implementation in §4.4. Do not compress it back to an absolute claim that guessing cannot work.
feedback.prior_round_status: Round-six CX010 fix confirmed in the current overview and §4.4.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, pointer paragraph
locator.quote: each zero of a non-marked column carries a back pointer to the marked column

feedback.feedback: This overstates the condition in the cited pointer function. ABBLSS require the designated highlighted zero (the leaf ℓ_j) in each nonmarked column to point back to the marked column; arbitrary other zero cells need not do so. Their algorithm explicitly allows the set of back-pointer destinations from all observed zeros to contain nonmarked columns. Thus replacing “highlighted zero” by “each zero” describes a different function.
feedback.why_it_matters: The entire comparison is meant to explain why earlier pointer constructions are easy for randomized algorithms. An inaccurate description of their positive inputs undermines that explanation and the credit to the predecessor.
feedback.advice: Restrict the claim to the highlighted leaf in each nonmarked column. Preserve the subsequent explanation of why finding arbitrary zeros yields candidate destinations rather than immediately identifying the marked column.
feedback.prior_round_status: Residual in the wording introduced to answer CX002. The old missing-tradeoff criticism is fixed; this is a new inaccuracy in the added description.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: a comparison between two losing columns can have any probability, including $1/2$

feedback.feedback: The contrast with a fixed graph and a bounded-error edge oracle is precise. It states a concrete interface difference instead of merely saying that the tournament is novel.
feedback.why_it_matters: This lets a classical separations reader understand why an existing fixed-tournament search theorem cannot simply be quoted unchanged.
feedback.advice: Retain the explicit 1/2 case and the distinction between certificate complexity and randomized complexity in the preceding sentences.

locator.quote: We cite, and do not reprove,

feedback.feedback: The explicit scope list is valuable. It now distinguishes the argument proved here from the Forrelation supplier, circuit and local-test ingredients, standard amplification facts, and the uniform refinement cited from the record.
feedback.why_it_matters: A referee can decide where independent source checking is needed; the list also prevents the phrase “complete argument” from being read as a promise to reprove the literature.
feedback.advice: Keep the scope statement, but make the abstract and contribution paragraph use the same convention. Do not expand it into a receipt or review-status ledger.

locator.quote: $\Phi=N/m^{(k+1)/2}$ for an integer $N$

feedback.feedback: The choice m=4^t has been fixed several times, but its useful role is never stated at the point of exact arithmetic: m^{(k+1)/2}=2^{t(k+1)} is integral for every k. That makes the displayed threshold tests comparisons of integers without parity cases.
feedback.why_it_matters: The apparently arbitrary restriction to powers of four otherwise looks like inherited notation rather than a simplifying design choice.
feedback.advice: Give the arithmetic reason for powers of four in a short clause here or at the initial parameter choice. The record already contains the needed explanation.

locator.quote: All of these are independent input bits.

feedback.feedback: In the definition of a total function there is no probability law yet. Here “independent” means freely assignable, disjoint input coordinates, whereas in §4 it means probabilistic independence under a carefully chosen law. Figure 1 similarly labels the instances independent.
feedback.why_it_matters: The lower bound relies on a precise distributional independence statement. Using the same word loosely in the construction makes that distinction harder to retain.
feedback.advice: Describe these as unconstrained or separate input coordinates. Reserve distributional independence for the hard experiment.

locator.quote: both bounds in (2) are proved for the function built from it

feedback.feedback: This is an essential short sentence. The function really depends on the circuit because the transcript bits are part of the input, and the paper now fixes one circuit for both analyses.
feedback.why_it_matters: Without it, a reader could mistake separate existential upper- and lower-bound constructions for bounds on the same total function.
feedback.advice: Keep the sentence, and keep the adjacent distinction that the classical lower bound uses circuit correctness whereas the quantum cost also uses circuit size.

feedback.feedback: This is a true input-length corollary for the fixed-k setting, but it is not used again and arrives between the definition and the local tests. It invites the reader to wonder whether a bound in terms of n is another advertised result.
feedback.why_it_matters: The construction already introduces several scales; the conversion to total input length interrupts the explanation of why certificates are locally checkable.
feedback.advice: Retain the polynomial input-size reassurance, but move the 1/44 consequence to a brief remark or omit it from the main flow. If kept, explicitly maintain the fixed-k qualification.

locator.quote: when $i$ does not win some test fails at $(i,s)$ for every address $s$

feedback.feedback: The universal quantifier over addresses is exactly the soundness statement the upper bound needs on arbitrary total inputs, including unpromised loser inputs. This is stronger and more useful than describing only the tests at the true address.
feedback.why_it_matters: It closes the otherwise tempting gap between a promise decoder and an algorithm for a total function.
